reasoning: The underlying problem — verifying whether an unlearned open model truly removed dangerous knowledge or merely hid it, by measuring recovery under small-scale relearning attacks on WMDP-style forget sets — is comprehensively covered by published work. BLUR (arXiv 2506.15699) is a public benchmark explicitly providing relearning datasets of varying difficulty for LLM unlearning robustness; "An Adversarial Perspective on Machine Unlearning for AI Safety" (2409.18025) and the benign-relearning paper (2406.13356) establish that fine-tuning on a handful of benign-adjacent examples recovers supposedly forgotten knowledge; and OpenUnlearning (2506.12618) is an existing packaged, drop-in framework for unified benchmarking of unlearning methods and metrics. The proposal's central metric (recovery curve / "fragility score") duplicates the established Accuracy Gap metric (post-relearning vs. original-model accuracy) and documented recovery-vs-relearning-examples dynamics. The only differentiating element is cosmetic packaging — single-GPU, afternoon-scale, single AUC summary score — which is a lightweight repackaging rather than a new contribution, so gaps are minor.

evidence.title: BLUR: A Benchmark for LLM Unlearning Robust to Forget-Retain Overlap
evidence.summary: Public benchmark that augments existing unlearning benchmarks with a suite of relearning datasets of varying difficulty and combined forget/retain queries to measure robustness; shows existing methods perform far worse under relearning. Directly instantiates the proposed 'public benchmark for unlearning robustness via relearning attacks.'

evidence.title: An Adversarial Perspective on Machine Unlearning for AI Safety
evidence.summary: Demonstrates that supposedly unlearned (e.g., RMU) dangerous knowledge on WMDP can be recovered via small fine-tuning and adaptive prompting, and that retrained models pick up 'forgotten' capabilities far faster than oracle models — the exact 'hidden vs. removed' question the proposal targets.

evidence.title: Unlearning or Obfuscating? Jogging the Memory of Unlearned LLMs via Benign Relearning
evidence.summary: Shows fine-tuning on small numbers of benign, topically-adjacent examples (low mutual information with the forget set) reverses unlearning and recovers forgotten knowledge — precisely the proposed relearning-attack methodology (5/20/50 benign-adjacent examples).

evidence.title: OpenUnlearning: Accelerating LLM Unlearning via Unified Benchmarking of Methods and Metrics
evidence.summary: An existing packaged, drop-in framework for unified benchmarking of LLM unlearning methods and metrics, including robustness evaluation — covers the 'shareable harness where others drop in a checkpoint' contribution.

evidence.title: Towards Robust Knowledge Unlearning: An Adversarial Framework for Assessing and Improving Unlearning Robustness in LLMs
evidence.summary: Defines the Accuracy Gap metric (post-relearning accuracy minus original-model accuracy) and evaluates recovery under small-portion forget-set relearning with learning-rate sweeps — equivalent to the proposed 'fragility score' / recovery-curve summarization.

evidence.title: Distillation Robustifies Unlearning
evidence.summary: Credible AF/LessWrong work treating relearning-attack recoverability as the standard robustness test for unlearning, confirming that retrained unlearned models recover capabilities far faster than models that never had them — the framing the proposal relies on is already mainstream.
